options: The practice of creating multiple classes with the same name
The ability of an object to take many forms, where a base class reference can point to derived class objects and call overridden methods
The process of converting one data type to another
A way to hide methods in a class hierarchy
questions.explanation: Polymorphism is the ability of an object to take on many forms. In C#, it is achieved through virtual/override methods and base class references. A base class reference pointing to a derived class object will call the derived class's overridden methods.

questions.prompt: Which keyword must be placed on a base class method to allow it to be overridden in a derived class?
Which keyword is used in a derived class method to replace a virtual base class method?
questions.explanation: The 'override' keyword is used in a derived class to indicate that a method replaces the virtual implementation from the base class. This enables the runtime to call the most derived version.

questions.prompt: Given: Animal a = new Dog(); a.Speak(); where Speak is virtual in Animal and overridden in Dog. What prints?
questions.explanation: With a virtual method overridden in Dog, a base class reference pointing to a Dog instance will call Dog's override at runtime. This is the core of polymorphism: the most derived implementation runs.

questions.prompt: Complete the declaration to hide a base class method named 'Show' in the derived class.
What is the difference between 'override' and 'new'?
options: There is no difference; both are the same
'override' performs compile-time polymorphism; 'new' performs runtime polymorphism
'override' provides runtime polymorphism; 'new' hides a method at compile-time
'override' is for fields; 'new' is for methods
questions.explanation: 'override' enables runtime (dynamic) polymorphism—the most derived implementation is called based on the actual object type. 'new' simply hides the base method at compile-time—it is selected based on the reference type, not the object type.
